name: Colin Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share-farm 220 hectares with an older couple, the Ashdowns, who own the land and want to stay on it without doing the work. I bring the labour and most of the machinery, they bring the land, and we split what it makes. It's wheat, oilseed rape and about 150 store cattle I buy in as youngsters and finish over the winter. In summer I also go out baling for six neighbours, which pays for the baler and a bit more. My partner Priya does the books at the vet practice in town, and the kids, Ravi and Asha, are thirteen and nine.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weather, mostly. You can plan all you like and then it rains for nine days in August. I'll use an AI chat thing now and then to check spray rules or ask about a weather window, but I double-check everything it says. I've been caught out by a confident answer before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd half expected that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, which is what I'd say about most things in the farming papers. I'd be fair about it, though. It does save a bit of time on the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the arrangement with the Ashdowns carries on, and the baling keeps paying. That's good. My worries would be the same as now: grain prices, fertiliser costs and whether Mr Ashdown's kids sell the land when he goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. I'd use the chat tool a bit more for the spray records, maybe. And we'd keep up the 180 a month savings and think about a newer baler in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing much changes, which is what I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the Ashdowns' kids.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are two, both in the city, both lovely, neither has any interest in farming. When their dad goes, they'll want their share out. That's the real threat to me, more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend that time saved on paperwork on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more paperwork, if I'm honest. There's always a new form. But maybe I'd get to one more of Ravi's football matches.

S0.say: It's useful but overhyped, like most things in the farming papers. To be fair, it does save a bit of time on paperwork.
S0.think: The arrangement with the Ashdowns carries on and the baling keeps paying. My real worries stay grain prices, fertiliser costs and whether the Ashdowns' children sell the land.
S0.do: Keeps going exactly as he is and uses the chat tool more for spray records. Keeps saving 180 a month and thinks about a newer baler in a couple of years.
S0.quote: When their dad goes, they'll want their share out. That's the real threat to me, more than any robot.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is careful and even-handed, praising and doubting AI in the same breath. His biggest worry sits outside technology: the landowners' heirs selling the land. He uses AI only with double-checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's probably the realistic one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers have always adapted and we'll adapt again. I'd also say you don't buy the first version of anything. Let someone else iron out the problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the baling goes first. Two of my six neighbours are already talking about a shared self-driving baler. That's maybe a third of my summer income gone, and I'd still be paying off my own baler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch who buys what and talk to the neighbours about a fair deal, maybe I run their shared machine for them. I'd save harder, 250 a month, in case the baling money drops. And I'd start using the AI tools properly for the cattle records, because that's the way it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the baling money I'd fret about, not the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the neighbours who buy the self-driving baler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good luck, and call me when it breaks down in a wet field. I'd mean it kindly, mostly. I'd be glad to be the man who knows how to get it going again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the farm itself you'd want to automate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the cattle feeding, once I've seen it work on three or four farms. Not before. I've seen a feed robot go wrong at a show and it was not pretty.

S1.say: Farmers have always adapted and we'll adapt again. But you don't buy the first version of anything; let someone else iron out the problems.
S1.think: The baling goes first. Two of my six neighbours are already talking about a shared self-driving baler, which is maybe a third of my summer income.
S1.do: Watches what neighbours buy and offers to run their shared baler for them. Saves harder at 250 a month and starts using AI tools properly for cattle records.
S1.feel: Uneasy about the baling income rather than the farm.
S1.quote: Good luck, and call me when it breaks down in a wet field.
S1.fieldNote: Colin pinpoints the most exposed part of his income: summer contract baling. His approach is to wait for proof and position himself as the person who can fix the machines. He'd automate only after seeing it work on several farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody could have planned for this, and I'd mean it. It's not the farmers' fault or even the government's, really. It just came too fast for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the share-farming deal falls apart. If the Ashdowns can get a robot to do my job for less than my share, their kids will push for it, and I couldn't blame them. The baling would be gone by the second summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the baler straight away while it's still worth something, maybe 18,000, and pay down the car loan. We'd cut the extras, so no new phone for Ravi, and the holiday becomes a weekend at Priya's parents. I'd ask the Ashdowns for a straight talk about the next three years, and I'd look at what help the farm support office offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops a bit just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sell the baler so early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in a year every baler in the country is for sale and they're worth nothing. Better to take a hit now than a bigger one later. It's the same with cattle, you sell before the market's flooded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Priya say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say her job's going too, because the AI does the books. Then we'd look at each other across the table and laugh, because what else do you do. Then she'd get the spreadsheet out.

S2.say: Nobody could have planned for this. It's not the farmers' fault or even the government's; it just came too fast for everyone.
S2.think: The share-farming deal falls apart if a robot can do my job for less than my share, and I couldn't blame the Ashdowns' kids for pushing it. The baling would be gone by the second summer.
S2.do: Sells the baler straight away for about 18,000 and pays off the car loan. Cuts extras including a new phone for Ravi and the holiday, asks the Ashdowns for a frank talk, and checks the farm support office for help.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with his stomach dropping as he says it.
S2.quote: Then we'd look at each other across the table and laugh, because what else do you do.
S2.fieldNote: Colin thinks like a trader under pressure: sell the baler before the market floods. He blames no one, seeing it as simply too fast. Both he and his partner, a bookkeeper, would be exposed at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's two or three seasons of watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to get ready but not to do anything daft. I'd say that at the discussion group I go to on the second Tuesday of the month. Someone always panics and buys something they regret.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd keep the share-farming going for three or four years, then it gets hard. If I'm the one who runs the robots for the Ashdowns, I might stay in. If I'm not, I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the baler two more summers and sell it in year three, before the price drops. I'd do a course in running and fixing farm robots once the first ones have proved themselves locally, probably year two. And we'd push savings up to 300 a month so we'd have a full six months when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels like I'd have a hand on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years you'd sell the baler at once. Why wait now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd still get two summers' baling money out of it. That's maybe 12,000 I'd lose by panicking. Timing's half of farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ravi and Asha?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That things are changing and they'll be fine if they keep learning. Ravi would be eighteen by then. I'd want him to have something practical he can do with his hands and his head, but I honestly don't know what that is anymore.

S3.say: It's time to get ready, but not to do anything daft. Someone always panics and buys something they regret.
S3.think: I'd keep the share-farming going for three or four years, then it gets hard. If I'm the one who runs the robots for the Ashdowns I might stay in, and if not I'm out.
S3.do: Keeps the baler for two more summers and sells it in year three. Takes a farm robot operation and repair course around year two, once the first robots have proven themselves locally, and raises savings to 300 a month.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a hand on the wheel.
S3.quote: That's maybe 12,000 I'd lose by panicking. Timing's half of farming.
S3.fieldNote: Colin uses the extra time exactly as a trader would, timing sales and training to the market. He'd retrain only once robots were proven nearby. He's honest about not knowing what to advise his son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper planning window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this sensibly. Train people up, try the machines, share them between farms. I'd say that at the discussion group and to the Ashdowns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fairly relaxed. I'd have time to see what works, buy in when it's proven and either run the farm with robots or move into fixing them. I'd be 53, which isn't too late to do something new if I start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd probably do nothing except watch. By year three I'd want a share in a robot feeder with two neighbours, maybe 8,000 my part. I'd do a robot repair course around year four and we'd start a small fund for Ravi and Asha's training, 60 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do nothing in year one. Is that a plan or putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, if I'm honest. But I've seen people buy the first robot milker in our area and spend two years fighting with it. I'd rather be the third person who buys one than the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in the area are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Ashdown, actually. He'd be in his late eighties by then. I'd want to sort out the share-farming deal properly with his kids long before then, so nobody's surprised.

S4.say: We've got time to do this sensibly: train people up, try the machines and share them between farms. I'd say that at the discussion group and to the Ashdowns.
S4.think: I'd be fairly relaxed, with time to buy in when things are proven and either run the farm with robots or move into fixing them. At 53 it isn't too late if I start early.
S4.do: Watches for the first year, then buys a share in a robot feeder with two neighbours around year three for about 8,000. Takes a robot repair course around year four and starts a 60-a-month fund for the children's training.
S4.feel: Uneasy at the back of his mind, but mostly fine.
S4.quote: I'd rather be the third person who buys one than the first.
S4.fieldNote: Colin admits his year of watching is partly delay. Ten years suits his wait-for-proof style, and he'd move to shared machines and repair skills. He'd also want to settle the share-farming agreement with the landowners' heirs early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the share-farming deal and the baling would both go before anything was proven. What would help is plain information about which machines actually work, and help to buy them jointly with neighbours instead of each farm going alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the land itself. Whoever owns the land does fine in all five of your pictures. People like me who just work it are the ones in the middle.

headlineQuote: Whoever owns the land does fine in all five of your pictures.
portrait: Colin Patel, 43, share-farms 220 hectares of wheat, oilseed rape and store cattle with an older landowning couple, and earns extra from summer contract baling. He uses AI now and then but double-checks it, and waits for proof before buying anything. He's calm if AI stalls, uneasy about losing baling income under steady change and alarmed by fast AGI, when he'd sell his baler at once. With five or ten years he times his sales, retraining and shared machine purchases carefully, blaming no one.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the share-farming deal and his baling work would go before any machine was proven.
whatWouldHelp: Plain information on which machines actually work, and help to buy them jointly with neighbouring farms.
